quickAnswer.question: What skills should a full stack developer put on a resume?
quickAnswer.answer: Full stack developer and full stack engineer roles look for one person who can own a feature end to end. Lead with a language you ship in both layers (JavaScript/TypeScript or Python), a frontend framework (React) and a backend framework (Node.js/Express or Django), then a solid database story (PostgreSQL plus Redis), API design (REST, GraphQL where relevant), and the delivery basics — Git, Docker, CI/CD and a cloud provider. As you grow, add system design, auth and security, and testing across the stack. Tailor the exact mix to the job you're targeting.

categories.title: Languages
categories.lead: Full stack is about owning both layers — lead with a language you ship in on both ends, and add depth in parentheses where you can, e.g. “TypeScript (React, Node)”.

categories.title: Frontend
categories.lead: The client half of the stack — list the frameworks and styling tools you've actually shipped interfaces with.

categories.title: Backend & Frameworks
categories.lead: The server half — the frameworks and runtimes you've built and operated services with, not everything you've read about.

categories.title: Databases & Data
categories.lead: Show depth where you've designed schemas and tuned real queries — full stack roles expect you to own the data layer too.

categories.title: APIs & Integration
categories.lead: How your frontend and backend talk — include the styles, auth and clients you've actually built with.

categories.title: Cloud & DevOps
categories.lead: Full stack increasingly means owning delivery — list the tools you genuinely operate day to day.

categories.title: Architecture & Design
categories.lead: The judgment skills that grow with seniority — claim the ones you can defend with real decisions.

categories.title: Testing & Quality
categories.lead: Full stack testing spans both ends — add the ones you've used on real projects, from unit to end-to-end.

categories.title: Tools & Workflow
categories.lead: The everyday tooling that keeps a full stack workflow moving — list what you use, not what you've merely opened once.

categories.title: Soft Skills
categories.lead: Choose 3–5 you can demonstrate through real work examples, not just claim — prove them in your experience bullets.

mistakes.title: Listing every framework you've ever touched.
mistakes.detail: A wall of 60 tools reads as noise. Curate to what you can defend across both layers.

mistakes.title: Only showing one side of the stack.
mistakes.detail: If your resume is all frontend or all backend, it reads as specialist, not full stack. Balance the two.

mistakes.title: Claiming scale or impact you can't quantify.
mistakes.detail: "Built scalable apps" is empty. Attach numbers — users, latency, load, conversion.

mistakes.title: Adding generic computer skills.
mistakes.detail: "Microsoft Office" and "email" are assumed and waste prime space.

mistakes.title: Listing skills you can't discuss in an interview.
mistakes.detail: Every skill on the page is fair game for deep-dive and system-design questions.

mistakes.title: Listing skills you never demonstrate in your experience.
mistakes.detail: Back each headline skill with a bullet that proves it.

skillsToAvoid.heading: Skills you usually don't need to list

faq.q: How many skills should a full stack developer put on a resume?
faq.a: Aim for 14–18 well-chosen skills. Enough to show both ends of the stack — a language, a frontend framework, a backend framework, databases, APIs and the cloud or delivery tools a job asks for — but curated to what you can actually discuss. A wall of 60 tools reads as noise and hides your strongest signals.

faq.q: Is a full stack developer the same as a full stack engineer?
faq.a: In most companies, yes — "full stack developer" and "full stack engineer" are used interchangeably, and job postings mix the two freely. "Engineer" sometimes signals a bit more emphasis on system design and scale, but the core skills are the same. Every skill on this page applies whether the posting says full stack developer or full stack engineer.

faq.q: What are the most important full stack developer skills?
faq.a: A language you ship in on both ends (JavaScript/TypeScript or Python), a frontend framework (React), a backend framework (Node.js/Express or Django), and a solid database story (PostgreSQL plus Redis) are the foundation. Beyond those, employers look for REST API design, testing across the stack, Git, Docker, CI/CD and a cloud provider — with system design growing in weight as you get more senior.

faq.q: Should I show both frontend and backend skills?
faq.a: Yes — that balance is the whole point of a full stack resume. If it's all React or all APIs, you read as a specialist. Group your skills so a recruiter sees both layers at a glance, and back it up with at least one experience bullet where you shipped a feature end to end, from database to UI.

faq.q: Which stack should I put on my full stack resume — MERN, MEAN, or something else?
faq.a: Name the stack you've actually shipped with, and make it concrete: "MERN (MongoDB, Express, React, Node)" or "React + Node + PostgreSQL". Recruiters and ATS scan for those specific technologies, so mirror the language of the roles you're targeting rather than listing a stack you only tried in a tutorial.

faq.q: What skills should a junior full stack developer include?
faq.a: Focus on the fundamentals you can demonstrate across both ends: JavaScript, React, Node.js, SQL and a relational database, Git, REST APIs and basic testing. Back each with a project or bullet. At entry level, one solid end-to-end project beats a long list of tools you've only tried once.

faq.q: How do I tailor full stack skills to a job description?
faq.a: Read the posting and note the specific skills it names — language, frontend framework, backend framework, databases, cloud. Mirror those in your own true words and move them toward the top of your skills section. Applicant tracking systems rank you partly on how well your resume echoes the job's language, so relevant, honest overlap matters.
